location.verification_method: Static read of lib/sinatra/base.rb at v3.0.3, v3.0.4, v2.2.2 and v2.2.3, the two fix patches, the helpers tests at v3.0.3/v3.0.4, and the saved advisory records. No Ruby code was run and no request was made.

critical_operation.code_excerpt:
params = format('; filename="%s"', File.basename(filename))
      response['Content-Disposition'] << params
critical_operation.description: attachment builds the Content-Disposition value by interpolating File.basename(filename) between the quotes of the filename parameter (line 405) and appends it to the response header (line 406). File.basename only strips directory components; it does not remove or encode a double quote, CR or LF. A filename such as `test.xml";\r\next=.txt` therefore closes the quoted string and appends attacker-chosen parameters (and a raw CRLF, where the server does not reject it), so the saved download name and disposition can be controlled. The fix escapes `"`, CR and LF to %22/%0D/%0A before interpolation; its regression test asserts the escaped header for exactly that filename.

entry_point.description: attachment is a public Sinatra helper. The advisory's precondition is an application that passes user-supplied input as the filename (directly, or via send_file's :filename option, which delegates to the same helper). The framework itself provides no route that reaches the helper with request data.

trace.description: the helper starts the header from the disposition and returns early when no filename was given
File.basename(filename) keeps quotes and CR/LF, and the value is formatted into filename="%s" without escaping
the unescaped fragment is appended to response['Content-Disposition'], so the quote/CRLF breakout reaches the outgoing header
send_file forwards opts[:filename] to attachment when a disposition is requested, so the same sink is reachable through the file-serving helper

source_crosscheck.notes: All three published sources carry the identical CVSS 3.1 8.8 HIGH vector and the same HIGH level; the CNA and NVD Primary scores are not mirrors of an OSV-derived number (NVD lists its own Primary metric). CWE-494 is published by the CNA and GHSA and repeated by NVD from the GitHub secondary source; no competing CWE is published. The affected ranges agree (>=2.0,<2.2.3 and >=3.0,<3.0.4) and the git blobs confirm v3.0.3 is vulnerable while v3.0.4 and v2.2.3 carry the fix.

limitations: Single-reviewer dossier; not eligible for data/vulnerabilities.jsonl yet.
No code was executed and no HTTP response was produced: the header injection is read from the string interpolation and the fix, not reproduced against a Rack server.
The advisory's precondition is an application that derives the filename from user input; Sinatra's own routes never call attachment with request data, so stock applications are not exposed.
Whether a raw CR/LF survives depends on the Rack server/proxy in front of the application; the quote breakout and the resulting filename manipulation do not depend on CRLF acceptance.
The 2.2.3 fix was content-verified only by blob identity and the backport patch; no 2.2.x runtime was exercised.
NVD publishes no Primary CWE; CWE-494 rests on the CNA and GHSA records. The classification as CWE-494 rather than a header-injection CWE is a source judgement, not independently re-derived.
No third-party reproduction or analysis was found in the saved sources; if none exists, the independent-evidence field will be false and the entry cannot reach grade A.
open_questions: Whether typical Rack versions in the affected range reject or strip CR/LF in response headers, which would reduce the impact to quote-only filename manipulation.

Whether the Reflected File Download impact requires the response body to contain attacker-controlled content in addition to the filename; the advisory frames it as an application pattern rather than a framework-internal route.
Whether the same unescaped helper is reachable through sinatra-contrib or other bundled extensions in ways the advisory does not enumerate.
